buildSteps.title: Choose a reachable nuclear transition
buildSteps.detail: Most nuclear levels need MeV photons, which no laser provides directly. Work focuses on unusually low-lying states, such as the thorium-229 isomer, whose energy sits near the vacuum-ultraviolet range.

buildSteps.title: Obtain a bright coherent source
buildSteps.detail: An X-ray free-electron laser or a synchrotron supplies short-wavelength pulses; for the lowest transitions, a frequency-comb laser delivering vacuum-ultraviolet light is used instead.

buildSteps.title: Prepare the nuclei in a host
buildSteps.detail: The isotope is embedded in a transparent crystal or a thin-film cavity so that many nuclei respond together and the optical response is strong enough to observe.

buildSteps.title: Deliver and focus the beam
buildSteps.detail: X-ray optics focus the pulse to a small spot and select a narrow energy band; for long-wavelength work, the sample sits inside the cavity.

buildSteps.title: Excite and read out
buildSteps.detail: The pulse drives the nuclear transition; the result is seen as re-emitted radiation, a change in transmission, or conversion electrons leaving the surface.

buildSteps.title: Control coherence
buildSteps.detail: Shaped pulse sequences are used to put the nuclei into a chosen quantum state and read it back — the same idea as quantum control of atoms, moved inside the nucleus.

buildSteps.title: Scale to patterned structures
buildSteps.detail: The speculative manufacturing step: arrange different nuclei in designed patterns so that a sample behaves as a device rather than a physics target.

prerequisites.why: they give the brief, intense, coherent short-wavelength pulses that make nuclear-scale experiments possible.

prerequisites.tech: Optical frequency combs and femtosecond timing
prerequisites.why: without precision timing and frequency control you cannot address a sharp nuclear line and measure it back.
only a handful of nuclei have transitions low enough to drive with available light; thorium-229 is the standout and was measured with laser light only in 2024.
mirrors, monochromators and cavities at these wavelengths lose much of the beam, limiting how precisely nuclei can be addressed.
no established method exists for assembling or altering nuclei as a manufacturing process.

pathway.milestone: probing and manipulating nuclear states with synchrotron and free-electron-laser beams, including X-ray studies of Mössbauer nuclei in thin-film cavities
pathway.unlocks: the ability to observe and partly control nuclear excitation with light.

pathway.milestone: the thorium-229 transition developed into a working nuclear clock
pathway.unlocks: far more precise timekeeping, improved satellite navigation and tests of fundamental physics.

pathway.milestone: reliable writing and reading of nuclear quantum states with shaped X-ray pulses
pathway.unlocks: coherent control of nuclei, the core skill any femtoscale engineering would need.

pathway.milestone: stored energy in nuclear isomers and patterned nuclear materials
pathway.unlocks: speculative ideas such as compact energy storage or designed nuclear samples — at present physics research, not a manufacturing route.
